title: The 2 Essential Principles of Effective Classroom Management https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2026/01/23/effective-classroom-management-principles/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin traces the two foundational principles behind SCM back to his own pre-teaching life experience, arguing they gave him an advantage his teacher education program never provided. The first, fun, he developed as a youth sports director, discovering that breaking activities into silly mini-games and injecting humor was what captured the attention of disengaged campers who had no natural interest in sports. The second, accountability, he credits to a series of mentors -- a coach who benched him, a father who withheld allowance, a professor who ejected him from an exam, and a demanding English teacher -- concluding that accountability only motivates when there's something the person genuinely wants, making 'want' the essential lever. His central claim is that fun creates the want, and accountability leverages that want into disciplined behavior, and that combining the two produced a smooth, peaceful first year of teaching despite his inexperience -- a formula SCM has since formalized into tested strategies.
points: Fun functions as the 'want-lever' that makes accountability actually work, since accountability only motivates when someone wants something enough to protect it.
Linsin traces the accountability principle to specific real mentors: a coach who benched him and a professor who threw him out of an exam for lateness.
The fun principle came from breaking baseball and basketball drills into silly mini-games to hold disengaged campers' attention.
Both principles combined produced an unusually smooth first year of teaching despite having no real training from his teacher-ed program.
quotes: When I first entered the classroom as a first-year teacher, I didn’t know what I was doing.
That is, until I found the secret to capturing and keeping their attention: Pure and simple fun. Fun is universal and will draw in even the most distracted future Goodall or Edison.
So I broke down every sport into miniature (and very silly) games. I told jokes. I imitated cartoon characters and embraced having fun myself.
The lesson wasn’t what these people did specifically. It was that accountability, when applied in a leveraged environment, was a powerful motivator.
Want is the key lever for accountability to work. Fun predictably provides that want-lever for every student.
Combined with a commitment to hold every student accountable for behavior that interrupted learning, I had a surprisingly smooth and peaceful first year of teaching.
